alt: An upright tree in the world forms a flat, upside-down image on the retina, yet we see a three-dimensional, upright tree. Sensation is the detection of physical energy by the sense organs; perception is the brain organising and interpreting it.
caption: Sensation detects; perception interprets and adds what the retinal image lacks.

alt: Four monocular cues with small pictures: height in plane (a boat near the horizon looks further away), relative size (a smaller car seems further), occlusion (a person in front of a door hides part of it) and linear perspective (railway lines meeting in the distance). Two binocular cues: retinal disparity and convergence. A note explains size constancy.
caption: Four monocular and two binocular cues let a flat image show depth.

after: ## Gibson's direct theory: the influence of nature
alt: A view from a train window. Fence posts close to the track flash past quickly in the opposite direction, shown by a thick arrow, while distant hills move slowly and seem to travel with you. Gibson argued the brain reads this difference in speed directly as distance. Strength and weakness cards follow.
caption: Near objects race past, distant ones creep: the speed difference is direct information about distance.

alt: Three line drawings: Rubin's vase, which can be seen as a vase or two faces; the Necker cube, which flips orientation; and the Kanizsa triangle, whose edges the brain fills in. A table groups illusions by explanation: ambiguity, fiction, misinterpreted depth cues with size constancy (Ponzo, Müller-Lyer) and misinterpreted depth cues (Ames Room).
caption: Illusions come from ambiguity, fiction, or depth cues and size constancy applied where they do not fit.

alt: Bruner and Minturn: an ambiguous figure shown between A and C was reported as B, and between 12 and 14 as 13. Cards cover motivation (hungry participants judged food pictures brighter), emotion, culture and the Müller-Lyer illusion, and an evaluation that both studies were artificial.
caption: Expectation, motivation, emotion and culture create a readiness to perceive in a particular way.
